claim: Transcranial electric stimulation aims to stimulate the brain by applying weak electrical currents at the scalp.
source: Transcranial electric stimulation aims to stimulate the brain by applying weak electrical currents at the scalp.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about TES presented in the abstract.

claim: When stimulating at 2 mA, cortical electric fields reach 0.8 V/m.
source: When stimulating at 2 mA, cortical electric fields reach 0.8 V/m, the lower limit of effectiveness in animal studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements and computational models presented in the study.

claim: 0.8 V/m is the lower limit of effectiveness in animal studies.
source: When stimulating at 2 mA, cortical electric fields reach 0.8 V/m, the lower limit of effectiveness in animal studies.
evidence: This references findings from animal studies cited elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: When individual whole-head anatomy is considered, the predicted electric field magnitudes correlate with the recorded values in cortical electrodes (r = 0.86).
source: When individual whole-head anatomy is considered, the predicted electric field magnitudes correlate with the recorded values in cortical (r = 0.86) and depth (r = 0.88) electrodes.
evidence: This correlation value is derived from comparing model predictions to intracranial recordings.

claim: When individual whole-head anatomy is considered, the predicted electric field magnitudes correlate with the recorded values in depth electrodes (r = 0.88).
source: When individual whole-head anatomy is considered, the predicted electric field magnitudes correlate with the recorded values in cortical (r = 0.86) and depth (r = 0.88) electrodes.
evidence: This correlation value is derived from comparing model predictions to intracranial recordings.

claim: Accurate models require adjustment of tissue conductivity values reported in the literature.
source: Accurate models require adjustment of tissue conductivity values reported in the literature, but accuracy is not improved when incorporating white matter anisotropy or different skull compartments.
evidence: This is based on the conductivity optimization procedure and comparison of model predictions with measurements.

claim: Model accuracy is not improved when incorporating white matter anisotropy.
source: Accurate models require adjustment of tissue conductivity values reported in the literature, but accuracy is not improved when incorporating white matter anisotropy or different skull compartments.
evidence: This is based on comparing models with and without DTI-derived anisotropy.

claim: Model accuracy is not improved when incorporating different skull compartments.
source: Accurate models require adjustment of tissue conductivity values reported in the literature, but accuracy is not improved when incorporating white matter anisotropy or different skull compartments.
evidence: This is based on comparing models with and without multiple skull compartments.

claim: This is the first study to validate and calibrate current-flow models with in vivo intracranial recordings in humans.
source: This is the first study to validate and calibrate current-flow models with in vivo intracranial recordings in humans, providing a solid foundation to target stimulation and interpret clinical trials.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study based on review of prior literature.

claim: Weak constant direct currents (tDCS, ≤2 mA) can elicit prolonged shifts in cortical excitability.
source: Weak constant direct currents (tDCS, ≤2 mA) can elicit prolonged shifts in cortical excitability (Nitsche and Paulus, 2000, 2001; Nitsche et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TES techniques have been investigated in over 70 neuropsychiatric conditions.
source: Because of their simplicity, flexibility and safety profile, these techniques have been investigated in over 70 neuropsychiatric conditions, including major depression (Bikson et al., 2008), epilepsy (Fregni et al., 2006d; Auvichayapat et al., 2013), tinnitus (Frank et al., 2012), Parkinson's disease (Fregni et al., 2006b), pain control (Fregni et al., 2006a, 2006c, 2007), and stroke rehabilitation (Schlaug et al., 2008; Baker et al., 2010) among others.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple clinical studies.

claim: Computational models have shown that the polarity of stimulation is necessarily mixed due to cortical folding.
source: Models have shown that the polarity of stimulation is necessarily mixed due to cortical folding.
evidence: This is based on prior computational modeling work.

claim: Nearby electrodes result in maximal electric fields between the two stimulation electrodes.
source: Furthermore, nearby electrodes result in maximal electric fields between the two stimulation electrodes (Datta et al., 2009), and not underneath the electrodes as commonly assumed.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior modeling work.

claim: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in the inter-hemispheric and ventricular spaces could guide current to deep structures of the brain.
source: Finally, these models predict that cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in the inter-hemispheric and ventricular spaces could guide current to deep structures of the brain (Datta et al., 2011; Senço et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a prediction from prior computational models.

claim: None of the computational model predictions have been directly validated to-date.
source: Unfortunately, despite increasing sophistication in these computational models (Wagner et al., 2004; Datta et al., 2009; Sadleir et al., 2010; Parazzini et al., 2011; Datta et al., 2012; Minhas et al., 2012; Datta et al., 2010; Wagner et al., 2007; Datta et al., 2011; Dmochowski et al., 2013; Luu et al., 2016), none of these model predictions have been directly validated to-date.
evidence: This is based on review of prior literature.

claim: Tissue conductivity values have only been measured ex vivo in other animal species.
source: Furthermore, the models depend heavily on tissue conductivity values, which have only been measured ex vivo in other animal species (Gabriel et al., 1996; Baumann et al., 1997; Oostendorp et al., 2000; Peters et al., 2001; Hoekema et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior measurement studies.

claim: Present estimates of electric field are at most 1 V/m.
source: This is of particular concern given that the present estimates (of at most 1 V/m) are at the lower end of what is required to affect neuronal activity in animal experiments (Reato et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on prior modeling estimates.

claim: Present estimates of electric field are at the lower end of what is required to affect neuronal activity in animal experiments.
source: This is of particular concern given that the present estimates (of at most 1 V/m) are at the lower end of what is required to affect neuronal activity in animal experiments (Reato et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to animal studies.

claim: The study recorded from 1380 intracranial electrodes in total.
source: In total we recorded from 1380 intracranial electrodes.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental data collected.

claim: Maximal electric field magnitudes are approximately 0.8 V/m when using 2 mA scalp stimulation.
source: For instance, we find that maximal electric field magnitudes are approximately 0.8 V/m when using the generally accepted maximum of 2 mA scalp stimulation.
evidence: This is based on the measurements and calibrated models.

claim: The low field intensities (0.8 V/m) are below the levels typically used in animal studies.
source: These low field intensities are below the levels typically used in animal studies providing a challenge to future studies on the mechanisms of action of TES.
evidence: This is based on comparison with animal study literature.

claim: All relevant measurement data have been made publicly available at http://dx.doi.org/10.6080/K0XW4GQ1.
source: To facilitate validation of new modeling approaches we have made all relevant measurement data publicly available (at http://dx.doi.org/10.6080/K0XW4GQ1).
evidence: This is a statement about data availability.

claim: Transcranial sinusoidal alternating current was applied to ten patients through two electrodes placed medially over the frontal and occipital pole.
source: Transcranial sinusoidal alternating current was applied to ten patients through two electrodes placed medially over the frontal and occipital pole (patients P03–P011 and P014, Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Measured voltages increased linearly with current intensity.
source: We first confirmed that measured voltages increased linearly with current intensity (Figure 3A; up to saturation levels of the clinical amplifiers).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A modest drop in magnitude (25% at 100 Hz) was observed with increasing frequency.
source: A modest drop in magnitude was observed with increasing frequency (25% at 100 Hz; Figure 3B), which we ascribe to a non-uniform gain across frequencies for the measurement equipment and electrodes as confirmed with recording of voltages in saline.
evidence: This is based on experimental measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The observed drop in voltage magnitude with frequency is ascribed to non-uniform gain across frequencies for the measurement equipment and electrodes.
source: A modest drop in magnitude was observed with increasing frequency (25% at 100 Hz; Figure 3B), which we ascribe to a non-uniform gain across frequencies for the measurement equipment and electrodes as confirmed with recording of voltages in saline.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on control measurements in saline.

claim: Uniform gain was observed for the tissue indicating purely resistive medium in the 1-100 Hz frequency range.
source: Thus, we observed uniform gain for the tissue indicating purely resistive medium in this frequency range.
evidence: This is inferred from the frequency response measurements.

claim: The variability observed in repeated measurements sets the lower limit in precision to ±0.11 mV for 1 mA stimulation.
source: Regardless, the variability observed here sets the lower limit in precision one can expect to ±0.11 mV for 1 mA stimulation (standard deviation pooled across electrodes and subjects; Figure 3C, values for P03).
evidence: This is calculated from repeated measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Subsequent recordings were performed at 1 Hz and with stimulation current of 0.25 mA to 1 mA.
source: Subsequent recordings were performed at 1 Hz and with stimulation current of 0.25 mA to 1 mA, limited by the dynamic range of the clinical amplifier and patient sensation.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: For subject P03, the measured voltages are tightly correlated across locations with the predicted electric potential values.
source: For this subject (P03) the measured voltages are tightly correlated across locations with the predicted electric potential values.
evidence: This is based on comparison of measurements with model predictions.

claim: High Pearson correlation coefficients (r = 0.94 ± 0.04) were obtained for all subjects between measured and predicted voltages.
source: The same is true for all subjects resulting in high Pearson correlation coefficients, r = 0.94 ± 0.04 (Here and in the following all summary statistics indicate mean and standard deviation across subjects).
evidence: This is calculated from the data across all subjects.

claim: The correlation of predicted and measured electric fields is lower than for the raw potentials.
source: As expected, the correlation of predicted and measured electric fields is lower than for the raw potentials (here r = 0.86, p = 10−14, N = 45), as the calculated field is the difference of two close-by measurements, each with some inherent noise.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Similar results (r = 0.81 ± 0.09) are obtained for all ten subjects for electric field correlation.
source: Similar results are obtained for all ten subjects (r = 0.81 ± 0.09), suggesting that the spatial distribution of electric field magnitudes is well predicted by the models.
evidence: This is calculated from data across all subjects.

claim: When collapsing all recordings across subjects, correlation between measured and predicted field projections is r = 0.86 (p = 10−118, N = 405) for cortical electrodes.
source: When collapsing all recordings across subjects (Figure 5F/G) we find correlation between measured and predicted field projections of r = 0.86 (p = 10−118, N = 405) and r = 0.88 (p = 10−54, N = 164) for cortical and depth electrodes respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from pooled data across all subjects.

claim: When collapsing all recordings across subjects, correlation between measured and predicted field projections is r = 0.88 (p = 10−54, N = 164) for depth electrodes.
source: When collapsing all recordings across subjects (Figure 5F/G) we find correlation between measured and predicted field projections of r = 0.86 (p = 10−118, N = 405) and r = 0.88 (p = 10−54, N = 164) for cortical and depth electrodes respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from pooled data across all subjects.

claim: Measured field projections in depth electrodes are nearly as strong as in cortical electrodes.
source: Note also that the measured field projections in depth electrodes are nearly as strong as in cortical electrodes (Figure 5F vs. Figure 5G; standard deviation of measured field projections across electrodes are 0.059 V/m and 0.065 V/m, respectively).
evidence: This is based on comparison of measurements from different electrode types.

claim: Maximal field intensities for the mid-line configuration are 0.28 V/m ± 0.06 V/m across the ten subjects for 1 mA stimulation.
source: Maximal field intensities for the mid-line configuration (Figure 1) are 0.28 V/m ± 0.06 V/m across the ten subjects (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is calculated from model predictions across subjects.

claim: For an intensity of 2 mA, the mid-line configuration would result in fields of 0.56 V/m.
source: For an intensity of 2 mA typically used in clinical trials this would result in fields of 0.56 V/m.
evidence: This is calculated by scaling the 1 mA results.

claim: For Subject P014 with electrodes away from the mid-line, maximum intensity on cortex for 1 mA stimulation was 0.25 V/m at the fronto-lateral location.
source: For other stimulation configurations on Subject P014 with electrodes away from the mid-line (Figure 2A, which is more typical for clinical interventions), maximum intensity on cortex for 1 mA stimulation was 0.25 V/m and 0.10 V/m at the fronto-lateral and lateral occipital locations respectively.
evidence: This is from model predictions for specific electrode configurations.

claim: For Subject P014 with electrodes away from the mid-line, maximum intensity on cortex for 1 mA stimulation was 0.10 V/m at the lateral occipital location.
source: For other stimulation configurations on Subject P014 with electrodes away from the mid-line (Figure 2A, which is more typical for clinical interventions), maximum intensity on cortex for 1 mA stimulation was 0.25 V/m and 0.10 V/m at the fronto-lateral and lateral occipital locations respectively.
evidence: This is from model predictions for specific electrode configurations.

claim: For three configurations tested, maximum field intensities in cortical locations was 0.38 V/m ± 0.09 V/m for 1 mA.
source: For the three configurations tested here, maximum field intensities in cortical locations was 0.38 V/m ± 0.09 V/m, again for 1 mA.
evidence: This is calculated from model predictions for different configurations.

claim: The 95th percentile of electric field intensity is 0.14 V/m ± 0.02 V/m for 1 mA stimulation.
source: To provide a sense of what intensities are reached in more extended areas (not just at the 1 mm3 voxel with largest value) Figure 6A also reports the 95th percentile (0.14 V/m ± 0.02 V/m), following previous practice (Parazzini et al., 2011; Alam et al., 2016).
evidence: This is calculated from model predictions following established methodology.

claim: Prediction error for maximal field intensities is in the order of 0.10 V/m.
source: Assuming that prediction accuracy scales linearly with predicted electric field intensity, this suggests that prediction error for maximal field intensities is in the order of 0.10 V/m.
evidence: This is estimated based on the spread of measured values and scaling assumptions.

claim: The mid-line electrode configuration results in significant current shunted through the highly conducting CSF in the inter-hemispheric fissure.
source: The configuration with both stimulation electrodes on the mid-line (Figure 1) is particular in that significant current is shunted through the highly conducting CSF in the inter-hemispheric fissure.
evidence: This is inferred from the model predictions and known conductivity properties.

claim: A relatively strong electric field may be produced in deep brain areas (e.g. peri-ventricular white matter and anterior cingulate) with the mid-line configuration.
source: As a result, a relatively strong electric field may be produced in deep brain areas (e.g. peri-ventricular white matter and anterior cingulate, see Figure 2D second row).
evidence: This is based on model predictions shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Deep brain areas may experience electric fields that are comparable in magnitude to the cortical surface.
source: The maximal values at a given depth summarized for all subjects and montages indicate that deep brain areas may experience electric fields that are comparable in magnitude to the cortical surface (Figure 6C, e.g. approximately midway between the center of the brain and the cortical surface (normalized distance 0.25) field magnitude were 0.21 ± 0.04 V/m for these 10 subjects with the mid-line montage).
evidence: This is based on analysis of model predictions as a function of depth.

claim: Conductivity values reported in the literature give similar estimates of the electric field magnitudes.
source: First, conductivity values reported in the literature used in existing models appear to give similar estimate of the electric field magnitudes (see values in 'Conductivity optimization').
evidence: This is based on comparison of model predictions using literature values with measurements.

claim: For Subject P03, measured electric field magnitudes were close to the predicted values with a slope s = 0.72.
source: For example, measured electric field magnitudes in Subject P03 were close to the predicted values, as indicated by the slope s = 0.72 of the best linear fit of the measured versus predicted field projections shown in Figure 7B.
evidence: This is calculated from the comparison of measurements and predictions.

claim: For voltage, the slope between measured and predicted values is s = 0.83 ± 0.24 across subjects using literature conductivities.
source: This is true for all subjects (for voltage: s = 0.83 ± 0.24; for field: s = 0.68 ± 0.21. Figure 8C/D under 'literature').
evidence: This is calculated from data across all subjects.

claim: For electric field, the slope between measured and predicted values is s = 0.68 ± 0.21 across subjects using literature conductivities.
source: This is true for all subjects (for voltage: s = 0.83 ± 0.24; for field: s = 0.68 ± 0.21. Figure 8C/D under 'literature').
evidence: This is calculated from data across all subjects.

claim: The model fitting appears to be under-constrained as differing parameters gave similar goodness of fit.
source: Generally the fitting procedure showed that the parameters are not tightly bounded by the data.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the optimization procedure.

claim: The median of the optimal conductivities are 0.03 ± 0.01 S/m for bone.
source: The median of the optimal conductivities are 0.03 ± 0.01 S/m for bone, 0.29 ± 0.10 S/m for skin, 0.38 ± 0.05 S/m for white matter and 0.82 S/m for gray matter (Figure 8E–G; ± indicates the median of the estimation uncertainty across subjects).
evidence: This is calculated from the optimization procedure across subjects.

claim: The median of the optimal conductivities are 0.29 ± 0.10 S/m for skin.
source: The median of the optimal conductivities are 0.03 ± 0.01 S/m for bone, 0.29 ± 0.10 S/m for skin, 0.38 ± 0.05 S/m for white matter and 0.82 S/m for gray matter (Figure 8E–G; ± indicates the median of the estimation uncertainty across subjects).
evidence: This is calculated from the optimization procedure across subjects.

claim: The median of the optimal conductivities are 0.38 ± 0.05 S/m for white matter.
source: The median of the optimal conductivities are 0.03 ± 0.01 S/m for bone, 0.29 ± 0.10 S/m for skin, 0.38 ± 0.05 S/m for white matter and 0.82 S/m for gray matter (Figure 8E–G; ± indicates the median of the estimation uncertainty across subjects).
evidence: This is calculated from the optimization procedure across subjects.

claim: The median of the optimal conductivities are 0.82 S/m for gray matter.
source: The median of the optimal conductivities are 0.03 ± 0.01 S/m for bone, 0.29 ± 0.10 S/m for skin, 0.38 ± 0.05 S/m for white matter and 0.82 S/m for gray matter (Figure 8E–G; ± indicates the median of the estimation uncertainty across subjects).
evidence: This is calculated from the optimization procedure across subjects.

claim: The optimal conductivities differ from the literature values but are largely in the same proportions.
source: These differ from the literature values (bone: 0.01 S/m; skin: 0.465 S/m; white: 0.126 S/m; gray: 0.276 S/m), but are largely in the same proportions.
evidence: This is based on comparison of optimized values with literature values.

claim: Models with median conductivity values give significantly better accuracy in predicting the electric field distribution compared to models using literature conductivities (t(12) = 2.36, p = 0.04).
source: Compared to models using literature conductivities, the models with median values across subjects give significantly better accuracy in terms of predicting the electric field distribution (pairwise t-test: t(12) = 2.36, p = 0.04, Figure 8B), but the magnitude is not significantly different (t(12) = 1.51, p = 0.16, Figure 8D).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of model predictions.

claim: The magnitude prediction is not significantly different between models with median conductivities and literature conductivities (t(12) = 1.51, p = 0.16).
source: Compared to models using literature conductivities, the models with median values across subjects give significantly better accuracy in terms of predicting the electric field distribution (pairwise t-test: t(12) = 2.36, p = 0.04, Figure 8B), but the magnitude is not significantly different (t(12) = 1.51, p = 0.16, Figure 8D).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of model predictions.

claim: Modeling individual anatomy is important for current-flow modeling.
source: This confirms that modeling individual anatomy is important.
evidence: This is based on comparison of predictions using correct vs. incorrect individual models.

claim: Correlation of recordings with predictions using a different head model is significantly worse compared to predicting values from the correct individual model (t(89) = 5.60, p = 10−7).
source: Correlation of recordings with these predictions using a different head model is significantly worse as compared to predicting values from the correct individual model (t-test on the difference between correlations: t(89) = 5.60, p = 10−7).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of model predictions.

claim: Extended field of view (FOV) gives significantly better predictions compared to the original FOV in terms of electric field magnitudes (t(10) = 6.17, p = 10-4).
source: This extended FOV gives significantly better predictions as compared to the original FOV, in terms of the electric field magnitudes (t(10) = 6.17, p = 10-4) and electric field distributions (t(10) = 2.63, p = 0.03; Figure 9B, comparing RMcut vs. RM).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of model predictions.

claim: Extended field of view (FOV) gives significantly better predictions compared to the original FOV in terms of electric field distributions (t(10) = 2.63, p = 0.03).
source: This extended FOV gives significantly better predictions as compared to the original FOV, in terms of the electric field magnitudes (t(10) = 6.17, p = 10-4) and electric field distributions (t(10) = 2.63, p = 0.03; Figure 9B, comparing RMcut vs. RM).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of model predictions.

claim: Removing the CSF compartment from the intact model did not significantly affect the distribution of estimated electric fields (t(12) = 1.78, p = 0.10).
source: We next tested the importance of CSF by removing the CSF compartment from the intact model – a model capturing the individual anatomy prior to craniotomy and electrode implantation. This did not significantly affect the distribution of estimated electric fields (Figure 9B, comparing correlations for IM vs. IM-CSF, t(12) = 1.78, p = 0.10), but did deteriorate the accuracy in predicting the magnitude of electric fields (comparing slopes, t(12) = 4.39, p = 10−4).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of model predictions.

claim: Removing the CSF compartment deteriorated the accuracy in predicting the magnitude of electric fields (t(12) = 4.39, p = 10−4).
source: We next tested the importance of CSF by removing the CSF compartment from the intact model – a model capturing the individual anatomy prior to craniotomy and electrode implantation. This did not significantly affect the distribution of estimated electric fields (Figure 9B, comparing correlations for IM vs. IM-CSF, t(12) = 1.78, p = 0.10), but did deteriorate the accuracy in predicting the magnitude of electric fields (comparing slopes, t(12) = 4.39, p = 10−4).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of model predictions.

claim: Incorporating heterogeneous conductivities for various bone compartments does not appear to provide a reliable improvement on magnitude estimates (t(12) = 1.72, p = 0.11).
source: Incorporating heterogeneous conductivities for various bone compartments does not appear to provide a reliable improvement on magnitude estimates (RM vs. RM + 3skull: t(12) = 1.72, p = 0.11), and it seems to give worse prediction on the electric field distribution (Figure 9B, RM vs. RM + 3skull: t(12) = 2.35, p = 0.04).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of model predictions.

claim: Incorporating heterogeneous conductivities for various bone compartments seems to give worse prediction on the electric field distribution (t(12) = 2.35, p = 0.04).
source: Incorporating heterogeneous conductivities for various bone compartments does not appear to provide a reliable improvement on magnitude estimates (RM vs. RM + 3skull: t(12) = 1.72, p = 0.11), and it seems to give worse prediction on the electric field distribution (Figure 9B, RM vs. RM + 3skull: t(12) = 2.35, p = 0.04).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of model predictions.

claim: There does not appear to be an obvious advantage to using DTI for three subjects with DTI data.
source: Three data points are not sufficient for a statistical comparison, but there does not appear to be an obvious advantage to using DTI.
evidence: This is based on visual inspection of results for three subjects.

claim: The intensities of electric field reach 0.8 V/m when using 2 mA transcranially.
source: Our main finding is that the intensities of electric field reach 0.8 V/m when using 2 mA transcranially.
evidence: This is the main finding based on measurements and calibrated models.

claim: The measured electric field intensity of 0.8 V/m at 2 mA is close to previous predictions using computational models.
source: This is close to previous predictions using computational models (Datta et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on comparison with prior modeling studies.

claim: Peak intensities are achieved underneath the stimulation electrodes.
source: Peak intensities are achieved underneath the stimulation electrodes, but also in deep midline structures such as the anterior cingulate and the peri-ventricular white matter for the specific configurations tested here.
evidence: This is based on analysis of model predictions.

claim: Peak intensities are also achieved in deep midline structures such as the anterior cingulate and the peri-ventricular white matter for the specific configurations tested.
source: Peak intensities are achieved underneath the stimulation electrodes, but also in deep midline structures such as the anterior cingulate and the peri-ventricular white matter for the specific configurations tested here.
evidence: This is based on analysis of model predictions.

claim: Individualized models provide predictions of the spatial distribution of currents with an accuracy of r = 0.86 for cortical electrodes when pooling data across all subjects.
source: We find that individualized models provide predictions of the spatial distribution of currents with an accuracy of r = 0.86 for cortical electrodes and r = 0.88 for depth electrodes when pooling data across all subjects.
evidence: This is calculated from pooled data across subjects.

claim: Individualized models provide predictions of the spatial distribution of currents with an accuracy of r = 0.88 for depth electrodes when pooling data across all subjects.
source: We find that individualized models provide predictions of the spatial distribution of currents with an accuracy of r = 0.86 for cortical electrodes and r = 0.88 for depth electrodes when pooling data across all subjects.
evidence: This is calculated from pooled data across subjects.

claim: The models capture individual anatomy for brain, CSF, skull, air cavities and skin at 1 mm3 resolution.
source: These models capture individual anatomy for brain, CSF, skull, air cavities and skin at 1 mm3 resolution.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach used.

claim: Extending the FOV to include the entire head and neck significantly improves prediction accuracy.
source: However, extending the FOV to include the entire head and neck significantly improves prediction accuracy.
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of models with and without extended FOV.

claim: Maximal stimulation intensity is difficult to measure directly because the recording electrodes are placed based on clinical considerations.
source: Maximal stimulation intensity is difficult to measure directly because the recording electrodes are placed based on clinical considerations, and are thus not arranged where maximal intensities are expected.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the experimental setup.

claim: Subdural electrodes allow measurement of the electric field only tangentially to the cortical surface.
source: Subdural electrodes allow measurement of the electric field only tangentially to the cortical surface, whereas strongest field magnitudes underneath the stimulating electrodes are oriented orthogonally to the cortical surface.
evidence: This is based on the geometry of electrode placement and field orientation.

claim: Electric field magnitudes in cortex can be as high as 0.4 V/m for 1 mA stimulation current.
source: Electric field magnitudes in cortex can be as high as 0.4 V/m for 1 mA stimulation current.
evidence: This is based on calibrated model predictions.

claim: For typical electrode configurations used in clinical trials maximal field intensity can reach 0.8 V/m when applying 2 mA.
source: For typical electrode configurations used in clinical trials maximal field intensity can reach 0.8 V/m when applying 2 mA.
evidence: This is based on calibrated model predictions.

claim: More extended areas can reach a value of 0.28 V/m (95th percentile) under 2 mA stimulation.
source: More extended areas can reach a value of 0.28 V/m (95th percentile) under 2 mA stimulation.
evidence: This is calculated from model predictions.

claim: For some electrode montages, current is shunted into deeper areas through highly conductive CSF with maximal values reaching 0.21 V/m.
source: For some electrode montages, current is shunted into deeper areas through highly conductive CSF with maximal values reaching 0.21 V/m.
evidence: This is based on model predictions for specific montages.

claim: The present data is broadly in agreement with previous modeling estimates with maximal intensities around 1 V/m.
source: The present data is broadly in agreement with previous modeling estimates with maximal intensities around 1 V/m (e.g., Datta et al., 2009) and 95th percentile of 0.35 V/m (e.g., Datta et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on comparison with prior modeling studies.

claim: Physiological effects in vitro have been found for electric fields as low as 0.2 V/m for entrainment of coherent gamma oscillations.
source: While physiological effects in vitro have been found for electric fields as low as 0.2 V/m (for entrainment of coherent gamma oscillations (Reato et al., 2010), other effects have required electric fields of at least 5 V/m (to entrain up/down state transitions (Fröhlich and McCormick, 2010); see Reato et al. (2013) for review on AC effects in vitro).
evidence: This is based on citations to prior in vitro studies.

claim: Other in vitro effects have required electric fields of at least 5 V/m to entrain up/down state transitions.
source: While physiological effects in vitro have been found for electric fields as low as 0.2 V/m (for entrainment of coherent gamma oscillations (Reato et al., 2010), other effects have required electric fields of at least 5 V/m (to entrain up/down state transitions (Fröhlich and McCormick, 2010); see Reato et al. (2013) for review on AC effects in vitro).
evidence: This is based on citations to prior in vitro studies.

claim: Plasticity effects have been demonstrated only at higher field intensities of ∼20 V/m.
source: Plasticity effects have been demonstrated only at higher field intensities of ∼20 V/m (Ranieri et al., 2012; Kronberg et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on citations to prior studies.

claim: Network effects may amplify electric field effects in vivo.
source: It is possible that network effects amplify electric field effects (Reato et al., 2010) and that larger neurons will be more strongly polarized (Radman et al., 2009) and thus, in vivo effects in human may be stronger than the effects demonstrated for animal in vitro experiments.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on cited prior work.

claim: Larger neurons will be more strongly polarized.
source: It is possible that network effects amplify electric field effects (Reato et al., 2010) and that larger neurons will be more strongly polarized (Radman et al., 2009) and thus, in vivo effects in human may be stronger than the effects demonstrated for animal in vitro experiments.
evidence: This is based on citation to prior work.

claim: A recent study reported the electric field produced by TES as measured by stereotactic EEG electrodes in two epilepsy surgical patients.
source: A recent study has reported the electric field produced by TES as measured by stereotactic EEG electrodes in two epilepsy surgical patients (Opitz et al., 2016).
evidence: This references a recent related study.

claim: Opitz et al. (2016) estimated maximal electric field to be 0.5 V/m with 1 mA TES.

claim: Extrapolating the accuracy of model predictions from the scalp surface to the brain is problematic given the ambiguity as to the amount of current entering the skull.

claim: After calibrating the models, the overall magnitudes of electric field were predicted with a single set of parameters across all subjects without a bias (s = 0.84 ± 0.31).

evidence: This is based on citations to prior literature.

source: The overall correlation of predicted and measured fields is 0.86 for cortical electrodes, and 0.88 for depth electrodes (Figure 5F/G).
